name: Platform-neutral procurement standards advocacy
consequences: Adopting platform-neutral procurement standards would reduce single-vendor dependence and create formal fallback trust anchors independent of Apple/Google; the trade-off is slower procurement cycles and higher oversight complexity as new paths must be validated.
options: Codify platform-neutral requirements in AltID procurement documents with explicit fallback-path clauses and a plan for independent trust anchors.
Create an open standards working group to publish interoperable wallet specifications aligned with NSIS, eIDAS2, and WebAuthn, inviting cross-agency adoption.
Develop a credible open-source reference implementation and formal certification guide to support vendor audits and procurement demonstrations.
review: Codifying platform-neutral requirements will shift risk to formal contracts, but may provoke negotiation delays and pushback from incumbents who benefit from current platform-control dynamics.

name: Coalition-driven resilience framing for digital identity
consequences: Formal governance coalitions increase political salience and resilience messaging, broadening support; however, they divert scarce resources from technical demonstrators and can slow decision cycles.
options: Establish a formal coalition comprising civil society, privacy groups, and policymakers to push resilience-focused procurement language.
Publish quarterly risk scenarios and resilience briefings to keep parliament and agencies informed and aligned behind platform-neutral principles.
Create an inter-ministerial oversight forum with defined decision gates and transparent milestones to reduce fragmentation in procurement policy.
review: Building a formal resilience coalition can elevate political support, yet it diverts scarce resources from technical work and may slow decision gates due to bureaucratic processes.

name: Credible non-production demonstrators for fallback trust
consequences: Phase-two demonstrators provide practical proof of standards-based fallback feasibility without production MitID integration; this can shift procurement discussions to technical feasibility, but may not fully address operational risk or scale considerations.
options: Develop a mobile-based FIDO2/WebAuthn demonstrator on GrapheneOS that authenticates against a simulated identity provider with open standards.
Create a browser-based or hardware-token fallback demonstrator to test non-mobile OS leverage, including cross-browser compatibility and user experience under privacy constraints.
Document the end-to-end demonstration architecture in a formal blueprint with risk controls and security review checkpoints for stakeholder scrutiny.
review: Non-production demonstrators credibly prove standards-based fallback feasibility, but they may not address real-world operations, scale, or sustained political pressure from platform incumbents.

name: AltID procurement language integration and EU alignment
consequences: Aligning with AltID procurement and EU wallet standards reduces lock-in risk and improves interoperability; however, it may require concessions on near-term performance metrics or vendor-specific features.
options: Embed platform-neutrality and fallback requirements into AltID procurement templates, with clear acceptance criteria and exit strategies.
Sponsor participation in European Digital Identity Wallet working groups to shape common interoperability and governance language.
Draft procurement pilots that test cross-border portability with pre-negotiated fallback pathways in incident scenarios.
review: Embedding AltID provisions and EU alignment strengthens interoperability, yet it may force concessions on near-term performance and vendor flexibility that incumbents resist.

name: Regulatory engagement and risk governance
consequences: Formal regulatory engagement deepens legitimacy and accelerates adoption of platform-neutral norms; yet it can provoke longer consultation periods and risk over-regulation that stifles experimentation.
options: Submit a formal policy proposal to Digitaliseringsstyrelsen outlining resilience, procurement neutrality, and fallback-path requirements.
Commission a regulatory impact assessment focusing on supplier concentration risk and continuity of service under platform disruptions.
Establish privacy-by-design review workflows integrated into every phase of demonstrator development and procurement planning.
review: Regulatory engagement lends legitimacy, but prolonged consultations and risk of over-regulation could slow experimentation and dampen agility in procurement and technology choices.

name: Staffing diversification and risk governance
consequences: A diversified team reduces single-point expertise risk and accelerates knowledge transfer; however, it increases management overhead and requires robust onboarding to maintain consistent security posture.
options: Implement cross-training programs ensuring multiple engineers can cover critical authentication components and demonstrations.
Establish a formal knowledge-transfer plan with staged handovers between researchers and contractor staff.
Pre-qualify multiple security-cleared contractors to provide rapid support for security reviews, testing, and incident response.
review: Staff diversification reduces single-expert risk and ensures continuity, but increases coordination overhead and requires disciplined onboarding to maintain security posture.

name: Platform-neutral access criteria codification in public procurement
consequences: Codifying platform-neutral access criteria creates a formal pathway that reduces single-vendor dependency and incentivizes suppliers to offer certified fallback mechanisms. Downstream, governance overhead increases and procurement timelines may lengthen due to heightened compliance reviews, while early supplier diversification can improve resilience in the medium term.
options: Redraft AltID procurement requirements to mandate platform-neutral fallback support and open-standard interoperability, with phased compliance milestones tied to risk assessments.
Institute a parallel procurement track for open-standard fallback components that is shielded from incumbent vendor negotiation dynamics to preserve neutrality and reduce lock-in.
Establish a neutral external certification body to assess platform-neutral claims and fallback readiness, with annual reviews and publish results.
review: Mandating platform-neutral procurement creates leverage to diversify suppliers, but risks delayed timelines and political pushback from established platform partners unless governance is tight and milestones are verifiable.

name: Non-production demonstrator governance and scale-up plan
consequences: Expanding the demonstrator portfolio strengthens credibility for fallback capabilities and standards-compliance, enabling evidence-based policy proposals. However, it increases budget pressure and may fragment focus if scope remains loosely bounded and milestones are not rigorously tracked.
options: Formalize a staged demonstration governance framework that expands to two additional OS/hardware stacks and documents test results in a public, citable repository.
Adopt a risk-managed expansion plan that preserves baseline credibility while setting clear criteria for exiting or scaling demonstrations if milestones fail.
Partner with academic consortia to conduct independent vulnerability assessments and publish findings that inform policy and procurement recommendations.
review: Expanding demonstrators boosts credibility and evidence quality but risks overextension and budget overruns if milestones are not tightly bounded and results are not promptly integrated into policy work.

name: EU-alignment voice through technical working groups
consequences: Early EU alignment can unlock interoperability funding and legitimizes Denmark's platform-neutral approach, but EU mandates may impose constraints that diverge from domestic priorities if not carefully reconciled.
options: Lead a Danish-position contribution to European Wallet interoperability standards, emphasizing platform-neutral fallback requirements and evidence from phase-one outputs.
Contribute targeted, data-driven inputs to EU policy dialogues to accelerate acceptance of fallback paths without compromising national sovereignty.
Establish a dual-track engagement: parallel national procurement policy development and EU standards alignment to hedge geopolitical and market risks.
review: EU-facing engagement promises credibility and potential funding, but it can dilute focus and slow domestic decision-making if EU timelines clash with national procurement cycles.

name: Domestic cryptographic hardware and token-based trust extension
consequences: Developing hardware-backed roots creates a local trust anchor and reduces exposure to platform-telemetry risk. However, it entails higher upfront costs and user onboarding friction, potentially slowing adoption.
options: Pilot alternative hardware tokens and secure enclaves as primary authentication devices integrated with AltID validations across multiple vendors.
Invest in open-source cryptographic libraries and vendor-neutral attestation services to reduce reliance on proprietary platform signals in fallback workflows.
Create a governance protocol to certify and rotate hardware roots across multiple suppliers, maintaining continuity during platform outages.
review: Pursuing hardware-backed roots strengthens sovereignty and resilience, but introduces procurement complexity and maintenance costs that must be offset by durable certification processes and robust supplier diversification.

name: Public resilience scenario planning and continuity funding
consequences: Develop scenario-based business cases comparing platform lock-in costs against fallback investments under geopolitical stress; this reframes resilience as a budget-anchored risk-management activity. It may face political resistance to re-allocating funds away from traditional modernization projects.
options: Develop scenario-based business cases that compare platform lock-in costs against platform-neutral fallback investments under varying geopolitical stress, ensuring decision-makers see tangible trade-offs.
Establish contingency budgeting rules that reserve funds exclusively for fallback authentication upgrades and supplier diversification activities with annual reviews.
Commission independent risk assessments and red-team exercises to stress-test fallback architectures and expose procurement blind spots before major procurement cycles.
review: Pairing resilience budgets with tangible trade-off analysis helps justify platform-neutral investments, but political resistance to diverting funds from core modernization can slow progress.

name: Transparent governance and accountability architecture
consequences: Establish open governance forums and publish decision gates; this improves legitimacy and stakeholder trust, but increases overhead and slows consensus-building among diverse actors.
options: Institute open governance forums with public reporting of decision gates, blockers, and progress toward platform-neutral criteria.
Publish anonymized risk registers and procurement decision matrices to enable civil society oversight without exposing sensitive vendor information.
Create annual external audits of supplier concentration risk and fallback readiness with published remediation plans and concrete improvement timelines.
review: Public reporting fosters accountability and legitimacy, but adds administrative burden and may invite political pressure that delays timely decisions unless governance processes are streamlined.

name: Fallback authentication architecture governance and certification path
consequences: Establishing a formal fallback path reduces platform lock-in risk by diversifying trust anchors and limiting single-vendor control. It also creates governance overhead and potential delays in procurement cycles if interoperability criteria prove more stringent than anticipated.
options: Mandate a platform-neutral fallback path with cross-service pilots to validate end-to-end interoperability across devices and browsers.
Incorporate procurement clauses requiring independent attestations and open-standard signals in AltID-related contracts.
Launch a phased rollout of fallback-capable authentication across high-risk public services and monitor performance and user impact.
review: Formal fallback governance stabilizes continuity but certification hurdles and cross-provider coordination may slow contract cycles and raise early-stage costs if interoperability milestones prove difficult.

name: EU interoperability advocacy for platform-agnostic identity anchors
consequences: EU interoperability advocacy can unlock portability and reduce vendor lock-in across member states, aligning procurement expectations with platform-neutral fallbacks. However, influence depends on long policy horizons and may provoke resistance from incumbent platforms that prefer centralized signals.
options: Submit formal contributions to EU Digital Identity Wallet working groups detailing platform-agnostic fallback requirements and portability guarantees.
Coordinate with Nordic partners to harmonize procurement language and certification criteria across jurisdictions to minimize duplication and accelerate adoption.
Publish technical notes that map open standards to secure identity workflows and demonstrate practical interoperability with existing MitID components.
review: EU-level engagement provides legitimacy and scale, but progress is slow and must contend with competing interests from incumbent platforms seeking to preserve market control.

name: Continuity-risk framing through stakeholder coalitions
consequences: Bringing civil-society, privacy advocates, researchers, and public servants into governance aligns incentives and resources toward resilience goals. It also risks slowing decision-making and triggering conflicts over data-sharing boundaries and accountability.
options: Convene civil-society, privacy advocates, academic researchers, and public-sector representatives to codify continuity requirements in AltID policy drafts.
Develop narrative materials that frame platform dependence as a continuity risk demanding robust fallback provisions.
Establish a governance charter with staged decision gates and explicit accountability for procurement changes.
review: Convincing a broad coalition improves legitimacy and buy-in, but it can create decision delays and conflict over competing priorities and transparency commitments.

name: Independent demonstrations validating platform-neutral fallback authentication
consequences: Technical demonstrations provide credibility for non-production approaches and help identify integration gaps early. However, a non-production scope may limit regulatory acceptance and can be attacked by opponents as insufficient evidence for real-world deployment.
options: Prototype a modular demonstration using WebAuthn and OpenID Connect on privacy-focused devices to illustrate interoperable fallback potential.
Create a publicly accessible test harness with clear security review checkpoints and interoperability criteria.
Translate demonstrator results into standardized procurement language and design documents for future bids, including compliance checklists.
review: Independent demonstrations offer credibility while avoiding the risks of production-scale deployment, but regulators may still demand live-system verification before procurement changes are approved.

name: Procurement architecture alignment for platform-agnostic identity anchors
consequences: Aligning procurement architecture reduces lock-in by embedding platform-agnostic anchors in bids, but it may provoke resistance from legacy suppliers and require substantial contract redesign. It also increases the upfront compliance workload for contracting authorities.
options: Draft tender templates requiring platform-agnostic identity anchors and explicit fallback requirements in AltID procurements.
Incorporate service-level remedies for outages tied to platform signals and ensure data portability rights across providers.
Run pilot procurement exercises comparing multiple fallback architectures and publish findings to inform ongoing policy decisions and supplier engagement.
review: Early procurement alignment reduces lock-in risk, but it invites pushback from entrenched suppliers who benefit from current platform dependencies and quiet lobbying.

name: Open-source reference implementation for platform-neutral authentication
consequences: An open-source reference implementation promotes transparency and peer verification, accelerating adoption and reducing bespoke vendor dependencies. It also requires ongoing governance, security audits, and commitment to maintenance beyond initial release.
options: Develop and release a modular reference implementation of fallback authentication using WebAuthn/OpenID Connect across devices.
Institute a community governance model with security reviews, contribution guidelines, and periodic audits.
Host international interoperability challenges to stress-test cross-provider compatibility and publish practical learnings.
review: Open-source reference code invites broad scrutiny and collaboration, but sustained security maintenance and governance are essential to prevent drift from official standards.
